subject: money
topic: Why your salary actually dictates your level of trust in neighbors
angle: While some studies link income inequality to lower trust, a large-scale analysis suggests that social class—not income inequality—is the actual predictor of social trust.
title: The Class of Trust

hooks.text: Does your income determine who you trust?
You assume inequality ruins trust. The data says it is your social class.
You are judging your neighbor through the lens of your own status.
A porch light flickers in the dark.
Social class dictates your level of trust.

reveal.headline: Social class is the primary predictor of your trust in others.
reveal.body: While income inequality is often blamed for low trust, a large-scale analysis shows that social class itself has a systematic positive effect on trust.

explain.headline: The evidence on income and trust is contested.
explain.body: Some studies link national income inequality to lower trust in others. However, other research finds the effects of income inequality to be nonsignificant. These findings are limited by how social class is measured.

matters.headline: Your position in the social hierarchy defines your outlook.
matters.body: That may be why your level of trust in your neighbors depends less on the wealth gap around you and more on your own social standing.

example.headline: You watch a neighbor through a cracked window.
example.body: You wonder if they are looking back. You weigh whether they are a friend or a stranger based on where you both live and what you do for work.

question.headline: Who do you trust in your own neighborhood?

stat.label: the effects of social class on social trust

claims.text: The effects of income inequality on social and institutional trust were systematically nonsignificant and smaller than the smallest negative effect of interest.
claims.quote: Second, the effects of income inequality on social and institutional trust were systematically nonsignificant and smaller than the smallest negative effect of interest.

claims.text: The effects of social class on social trust were systematically positive.
claims.quote: First, the effects of social class on social trust were systematically positive, whereas the effects on institutional trust depended on the way social class was measured.

claims.text: The negative link between income inequality and the happiness of lower-income respondents was explained not by lower household income, but by perceived unfairness and lack of trust.
claims.quote: Most important, we found that the negative link between income inequality and the happiness of lower-income respondents was explained not by lower household income, but by perceived unfairness and lack of trust.

claims.text: Americans trusted other people less in years with more national income inequality than in years with less national income inequality.
claims.quote: Americans trusted other people less and perceived other people to be less fair in the years with more national income inequality than in the years with less national income inequality.

claims.text: Lack of trust is more common in more unequal societies.
claims.quote: Recent evidence suggests that many other social problems, including mental illness, violence, imprisonment, lack of trust, teenage births, obesity, drug abuse, and poor educational performance of schoolchildren, are also more common in more unequal societies.

verdict: The evidence is contradictory, as one study finds income inequality linked to lower trust while a larger study finds the effect of income inequality on trust to be nonsignificant.
caveat: The findings are limited by inconsistencies in how social class is measured and the small number of higher-level units available in some research.
caption:
Your social standing shapes your perception of the people around you.

Research shows that while income inequality is often linked to lower trust, larger analyses find the effect to be nonsignificant. Instead, social class appears to be a systematic predictor of trust, though results remain mixed due to measurement inconsistencies.

How much of your trust in others is based on your own social position?
